title: Changing environments
keyIdea: Environments change. Some changes are fast, like a fire or a flood. Some are slow, like a pond drying over a summer or a mountain slowly getting warmer. When a place changes, its living things do not all have the same fate. Some survive there. Some move away to a place that still meets their needs. Some new living things move in. And some die, because they cannot move and the place no longer gives them what they need. A change can also pass along a food chain: a drought kills grass, then rabbits go hungry, then foxes have less to eat. Living things cannot change their bodies because they need to; that takes many generations.
familyTip: Look at a patch of ground near you: a puddle, a cut lawn or a pile of leaves. Ask what would happen to the minibeasts and plants there if it dried up, flooded or was dug up. Which could move away? Which would die? What might move in?

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort a drying pond, warm a mountain, sort what a fire does, order the regrowth, and follow a drought along a food chain.

kid: A pond dries up in a hot summer. The fish need water to breathe and cannot walk to another pond, so most of them die. Water lilies are stuck in the mud, so they die too. Ducks and dragonflies can fly, so they move away to find water.

But a change is not bad for everyone. Grass seeds blow onto the dry mud and grow. Then rabbits come to eat the grass. They move in. So when a place changes, some living things survive, some move away, some move in and some die.

Some changes are slow. When a mountain gets warmer, trees grow higher up its sides. Pikas are small furry animals that need cold, so they move up too. If it keeps warming, they reach the top and have nowhere left to go.

One change can spread. A drought kills grass. Rabbits eat grass, so there are fewer rabbits. Foxes eat rabbits, so a year later there are fewer foxes too. An animal cannot just grow a new body to fit the change. That takes a very long time.
adult: Ages 8 to 9. NGSS 3-LS4-4 asks pupils to argue that when an environment changes, some organisms survive and reproduce, some move to new locations, some move into the changed environment, and some die. The National Curriculum in England, Year 4 living things and their habitats, asks pupils to recognise that environments can change and that this can sometimes pose dangers to living things. This lesson covers natural changes as well as warming; human causes such as deforestation are taught in the separate human-impact lesson.

The lab gives each outcome a concrete case. A drying pond sorts six organisms by whether they can move and what they need. A warming mountain shows an upslope range shift, as recorded for American pikas in the Great Basin and for treelines worldwide. A forest fire produces all four outcomes, including newcomers such as fireweed and black-backed woodpeckers. Pupils then order the regrowth stages after the fire, and follow a drought along a grass, rabbit and fox food chain.

Common mistakes. Many children think a living thing can change its body because it needs to, such as fish growing legs when a pond dries; adaptation by natural selection takes many generations. Some think every change harms every organism, and miss the ones that move in. Others think plants can move away, or that a change only affects animals that eat the lost food directly. The bar charts in the food-chain step are a simple model, not field data.

practice.prompt: A pond dries up. Why can ducks survive but water lilies cannot?
choices: Ducks can fly away; lilies are rooted in the mud
practice.hint: Think about which one can move to a new pond.
practice.explain: Ducks fly to another pond. A lily is rooted in the mud and needs water, so it dies when the pond dries.

practice.prompt: A drought kills the grass in year {a}. Rabbits fall the next year. Foxes fall the year after that. In which year do the foxes fall?
practice.hint: Count one year for the rabbits and one more for the foxes.
practice.explain: Grass falls in year {a}, rabbits in year {=a+1} and foxes in year {=a+2}. The change moves one step along the food chain each year in this model.

practice.prompt: After a forest fire, which living thing is most likely to move in?
choices: Fireweed, whose seeds blow in on the wind
practice.hint: Which one can arrive fast and grows well in sunny, burnt ground?
practice.explain: Fireweed seeds float in on the wind and grow quickly in the open, sunny ground. Tall trees take many years, and fish need water.

practice.prompt: It gets about 1 °C cooler for every 150 m you climb a mountain. If the mountain warms by {a} °C, about how many metres higher must a pika live to stay as cool?
practice.hint: Each 1 °C of warming means 150 m higher. Multiply.
practice.explain: {a} × 150 m = {=150*a} m. Cold-loving animals like the pika move uphill as their home warms.

practice.prompt: A river floods a field for months. Which animal is worse off?
choices: A mole that digs in dry soil
practice.hint: Which animal needs dry ground to live?
practice.explain: Moles dig tunnels in dry soil, so a flood takes away their home. Frogs and ducks do well in wet places.

pool.prompt: When an environment changes, which list shows what can happen to living things?
choices: Survive, move away, move in or die
pool.hint: Think of the drying pond: fish, ducks and grass.
pool.explain: Some survive, some move away, some move in and some die. Different living things have different fates.

pool.prompt: Sam says fish in a drying pond will grow legs so they can walk away. What is wrong?
choices: A body cannot change because it needs to; that takes many generations
pool.hint: Can one fish change its body in a summer?
pool.explain: Living things cannot change their bodies just because they need to. Changes in a kind of living thing happen over many generations, far too slowly to escape a drying pond.

pool.prompt: A mountain gets warmer. Where do cold-loving alpine flowers end up growing?
pool.hint: Is it cooler at the top or at the bottom?
pool.explain: It is cooler higher up. As the mountain warms, cold-loving plants only grow higher up, so their zone moves uphill and shrinks.

pool.prompt: Foxes eat rabbits. Rabbits eat grass. A drought kills the grass. What happens to the foxes?
choices: There are fewer foxes, a little later
Nothing, because foxes do not eat grass
pool.hint: Follow the food chain one step at a time.
pool.explain: Less grass means fewer rabbits. Fewer rabbits means less food for foxes, so the fox numbers fall too, a bit later.

pool.prompt: After a fire, what grows back first?
choices: Fast plants like fireweed and grasses
pool.hint: What can grow in one season?
pool.explain: Fast plants come first in the sunny, burnt ground. Shrubs follow, then young trees, and a tall forest takes many years.

pool.prompt: Which change is a fast change?
choices: A pond slowly filling with mud
pool.hint: Which one happens in a day or two?
pool.explain: A fire changes a forest in days. Warming and filling with mud take years.

pool.prompt: A beaver dam floods a dry wood. Which animal is most likely to move in?
choices: Ground beetles that need dry leaves
pool.explain: The new pond gives ducks water and food, so they move in. Moles and dry-ground beetles lose their homes.

pool.prompt: A pond had {=a+b} kinds of animal. After it dried up, 2 new kinds moved in and {a} of the old kinds moved away or died. How many of the old kinds survived there?
pool.hint: Take the ones that left or died away from the old total. The 2 new kinds are not old kinds.
pool.explain: {=a+b} − {a} = {b}. {b} of the old kinds stayed and survived. The 2 kinds that moved in are new arrivals, so they do not count.

pool.prompt: Pikas on a mountain live at about 2400 m. It is about 1 °C cooler for every 150 m higher. If the mountain warms by {a} °C, about how high must the pikas live to stay as cool?
pool.hint: Work out how far up {a} °C of warming pushes them, then add it to 2400 m.
pool.explain: {a} × 150 m = {=150*a} m higher, so about 2400 + {=150*a} = {=2400+150*a} m. If the mountain is not that tall, the pikas run out of room.
